typical_mindset: Acute and obtuse are remembered as a pair of opposite labels without a firm anchor to which one means 'smaller than a right angle' and which means 'bigger' — the labels get swapped even when the underlying comparison-to-90-degrees idea is understood.
explanation_strategy: Anchor both labels to the right angle (90 degrees) as the dividing line, using a concrete comparison, rather than asking the child to recall the definitions directly.

example_dialogue.text: Is this angle bigger or smaller than a right angle (like the corner of a book)?
Right — angles smaller than a right angle are called acute. So what would you call this one?

source: Topic-authored; no direct literature-survey citation for acute/obtuse label confusion specifically.

typical_mindset: A right angle (a square corner, 90 degrees) and a straight angle (a flat line, 180 degrees) are both remembered as 'the special named angles' without a firm sense of just how different their sizes are — the labels get swapped even though a right angle looks nothing like a flat line once actually pictured.
explanation_strategy: Ground both labels in a concrete, physical comparison — a square corner versus a flat ruler laid down — rather than asking the child to recall the definitions by name.

example_dialogue.text: Does this angle look like the corner of a square book, or like a flat, straight line?
Right — a flat line like that is called a straight angle. So is it a right angle, or a straight angle?

source: Topic-authored; no direct literature-survey citation for right/straight angle label confusion specifically.

typical_mindset: When naming a polygon by its number of sides (triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon), the child counts corners instead of sides, or loses count partway around an irregular-looking shape, landing on a neighboring polygon name instead of the correct one.
explanation_strategy: Have the child trace each side with a finger while counting out loud, one side at a time, starting from a marked point and stopping exactly when they return to it, rather than glancing at the shape and guessing its name.

example_dialogue.text: Let's trace and count together, starting from this corner. One side... two sides... keep going until we get back to where we started.
Five sides — so what do we call a shape with five sides?

source: NCERT Class 5 Ch.2 misconception notes — not matched to a deterministic buggy-rule signature (miscounting is a slip on the child's own counting process, not a stable field-comparable pattern against the correct answer).
